docs.title: Welcome to CapivaraOS Docs
docs.text:
CapivaraOS is a family of Fedora-based Linux distributions built for developers: secure by default, with local AI and a full development environment ready at first boot.

These docs cover Series 2, built on Fedora 45. Documentation for earlier releases is still available in the Archive.

docs.title: Choose your distro
docs.text:
Distro Desktop Profile Marsh KDE Plasma 6.8 The flagship edition, highly customizable Pup Xfce 4.20 Light and fast, without giving up the toolkit Snout GNOME 51 Clean and direct, with no layout changes

All three ship the same toolkit and the same two exclusive applications: COS Dev Center and COS Config Center.

docs.title: Server: Herd by CapivaraOS
docs.text: Need a server? Herd by CapivaraOS is the headless line (no desktop) for physical machines, VMs and the cloud — with Cockpit, hardened security and compliance out of the box. See the Herd documentation.

docs.title: Changelog
docs.text:
Key milestones in the development of CapivaraOS's distros.

This changelog only covers CapivaraOS's branding and system tweaks — it doesn't include the upstream Fedora, KDE, Xfce or GNOME package history.

November 2026

The first release of Series 2, rebuilt on Fedora 45 with KDE Plasma 6.8 on a Wayland session.

New

  • Upgrades without reinstalling. From this release on, the system moves between versions and between generations in place, through the software centre or the terminal, from a signed repository. A snapshot is taken before each generation upgrade. See Keeping your system updated. (FEAT-111)
  • COS Dev Center, which opens at first boot and sets up the workstation: local AI on your own machine, language tracks, dev tools and GitHub. (FEAT-90)
  • COS Config Center, with nine modules that handle graphically what used to need a terminal — codecs, keyboard, language, firewall, disks, network, cleanup, logs and diagnostics. (PROD-5)
  • A visual identity of our own from boot to desktop: boot splash, boot menu, icons and theme, with an exclusive wallpaper collection. On Marsh the wallpaper changes with the time of day. (FEAT-91, FEAT-132)
  • The media boot menu now shows the CapivaraOS version alongside Fedora's.

Fixed

  • On an encrypted disk (LUKS), the boot splash drew no password field: the system looked frozen on the capybara image, and the password could only be typed by dropping to text mode. (BUG-45)
  • The default wallpaper was not applied on Fedora 45 and the desktop fell back to Plasma's stock wallpaper.
  • The computer name came up as localhost-live instead of capivaraos. A name you choose yourself is still respected.
  • fastfetch showed only the capybara, without the system information beside it. (FEAT-136)
  • The installer's final screen no longer shows the feedback block with a QR code pointing outside the project. (FEAT-145)

August 2026

  • Fix: CapivaraOS Marsh now installs on computers with UEFI firmware. Previously the installation went almost all the way and then failed at the bootloader step, because the installer did not recognize CapivaraOS as its own profile and looked for the boot files in the wrong place. (BUG-38)
  • Fix: the installed system now boots on a wider range of hardware (for example, netbooks with eMMC storage). Previously, on machines whose storage differed from the one used to build the image, the system could fail to find the disk on first boot and drop into emergency mode. (BUG-40)

August 2026

  • Minor licensing fixes to the photo wallpapers.

July 2026

  • New visual identity: the walking capybara logo across all branding — wallpapers, icons, boot splash, login screen and installer. (DOC-6)
  • The dock's application launcher icon is now the capybara head, replacing the KDE logo. (DOC-6)
  • Fix: the logo no longer overlaps the text on the live session's welcome screen.
  • Fix: the ISO now ships with Fedora updates included, avoiding roughly 1,000 update packages on first boot.
  • Fix: the logo and photo credit on the photographic wallpapers are no longer cropped off on 4:3 screens.
  • Fix: the logo artwork no longer shows up as an option in the wallpaper picker.

June 2026

  • Plymouth now works correctly — boot animation with the CapivaraOS logo displays properly (fix: missing plymouth-plugin-script package).
  • GRUB title stays correct — boot menu permanently shows "CapivaraOS Marsh", even after system updates.
  • Offline update screen — Plymouth shows progress percentage during boot-time updates.
  • Fixed a brief duplicate bottom dock appearing right after login.
  • Plasma's welcome screen no longer opens on first login.

June 2026

  • First release ported to Fedora 44, from the original Debian/trixie base.

November 2026

The first release of Series 2, on Fedora 45 with Xfce 4.20.

New

  • Upgrades without reinstalling, with a signed repository and a snapshot before each generation upgrade. See Keeping your system updated. (FEAT-111)
  • COS Dev Center and COS Config Center, the same as the other editions — Pup is light, not cut down.
  • A new default wallpaper, "rio", with capybaras in the river, exclusive to Pup.
  • The media boot menu now shows the CapivaraOS version.

Fixed

  • On an encrypted disk (LUKS), the boot splash drew no password field and the system looked frozen. (BUG-46)
  • The computer name came up as localhost-live instead of capivaraos.
  • fastfetch showed only the capybara, without the system information.
  • The installer's final screen no longer shows the feedback block with a QR code. (FEAT-145)
  • Fixed the logo placement on the "rio" wallpaper.

Day-to-day updates on Pup

On Fedora 45, Xfce's graphical updater does not list our updates — a limitation of that component, not of the repository. On Pup, use sudo dnf upgrade --refresh. Details in Keeping your system updated.

August 2026

  • Fix: CapivaraOS Pup now installs on computers with UEFI firmware. Previously the installation went almost all the way and then failed at the bootloader step, because the installer did not recognize CapivaraOS as its own profile and looked for the boot files in the wrong place. (BUG-38)
  • Fix: the installed system now boots on a wider range of hardware (for example, netbooks with eMMC storage). Previously, on machines whose storage differed from the one used to build the image, the system could fail to find the disk on first boot and drop into emergency mode. (BUG-40)

August 2026

  • Fix: the CapivaraOS wallpaper is now applied automatically on the first login (live and installed). Previously you had to change it manually once for it to stick.

July 2026

  • First public beta release of Pup, available to download.
  • New visual identity: the walking capybara logo across all branding — wallpapers, icons, boot splash, login screen and installer. (DOC-6)
  • Fix: the ISO now ships with Fedora updates included. The updates repository was being silently ignored because it used a name reserved by Anaconda, so images shipped with plain Fedora 44.
  • Fix: the logo and photo credit on the photographic wallpapers are no longer cropped off on 4:3 screens.
  • Fix: the system identification in os-release and GRUB now survives future Fedora updates.

June 2026

  • First release of the Xfce spin (Fedora 44), designed for computers with at least 4 GB of RAM.
  • Exclusive wallpapers: 13 solid-color backgrounds with the CapivaraOS logo, plus capybara photos from Wikimedia Commons (CC BY/CC BY-SA) with embedded credits.
  • Full branding in the graphical installer — shows CapivaraOS logo and colors instead of Fedora's.
  • Custom Plymouth boot theme on startup and shutdown.
  • LightDM login screen with CapivaraOS visual identity.
  • System correctly identified as CapivaraOS Pup in os-release and GRUB.

November 2026

The first release of Series 2, on Fedora 45 with GNOME 51 on a Wayland session, with no layout modifications.

New

  • Upgrades without reinstalling, with a signed repository and a snapshot before each generation upgrade. See Keeping your system updated. (FEAT-111)
  • COS Dev Center and COS Config Center.
  • An icon set of our own, curated extensions and an exclusive wallpaper collection, including one only Snout has.

Fixed

  • On an encrypted disk (LUKS), the boot splash drew no password field and the system looked frozen. (BUG-45)
  • The computer name came up as localhost-live instead of capivaraos.
  • fastfetch showed only the capybara, without the system information.
  • The installer's final screen no longer shows the feedback block with a QR code. (FEAT-145)

August 2026

  • Fix: the login screen shows up correctly again. Previously, when automatic login was turned off, the system did not show the login screen and instead entered an empty session — with no user list and no password field —, and in that state the Terminal could not be opened. Cause: a missing line in the GNOME login screen configuration, introduced when customizing the login wallpaper. (BUG-42)
  • The Terminal now comes pinned to the app dock for easier access.

August 2026

  • Fix: CapivaraOS Snout now installs on computers with UEFI firmware. Previously the installation went almost all the way and then failed at the bootloader step, because the installer did not recognize CapivaraOS as its own profile and looked for the boot files in the wrong place. (BUG-38)
  • Fix: the installed system now boots on a wider range of hardware (for example, netbooks with eMMC storage). Previously, on machines whose storage differed from the one used to build the image, the system could fail to find the disk on first boot and drop into emergency mode. (BUG-40)

August 2026

  • Minor licensing fixes to the photo wallpapers.

July 2026

  • First public beta release of Snout, available to download.
  • New visual identity: the walking capybara logo across all branding — wallpapers, icons, boot splash, GDM login screen and installer. (DOC-6)
  • Fix: the ISO now ships with Fedora updates included. The updates repository was being silently ignored because it used a name reserved by Anaconda.
  • Fix: the logo in GNOME's "About" panel is no longer cropped at the edges.
  • Fix: the system identification and the CapivaraOS logo now survive future Fedora updates — three mechanisms meant to reapply them were never actually running.

June 2026

  • First release of the GNOME spin, with its own branding package (capivaraos-branding), wallpapers, boot/login theme, and GDM background via dconf.
  • Stock Fedora Workstation GNOME environment, with no dock, global menu, or third-party themes.

August 2026

  • One-command hardening: new herd-harden, which applies SCAP Security Guide profiles (OSPP, CIS, PCI-DSS) via Ansible, with a dry-run preview by default. (FEAT-97)
  • Compliance report with evidence: herd-compliance-scan now accepts profile aliases and also produces an ARF file (auditing evidence), alongside HTML/XML. (FEAT-97)
  • FIPS mode documented for Fedora 44 (via fips=1 on the kernel) and disk encryption (LUKS) as opt-in options.
  • The line is now branded Herd by CapivaraOS.

August 2026

  • First stable release of the server line: headless Fedora 44 base, SELinux enforcing, hardened SSH, restrictive firewall, auditing on, and the Cockpit web console included. (PROD-4)
  • qcow2 images (cloud/cloud-init) and a branded installer ISO (x86_64). (PROD-4)

docs.title: How to contribute
docs.text: CapivaraOS is an open source project and all help is welcome.

docs.title: Documentation
docs.text:
This documentation lives in the capivaraos-docs repository. To propose a fix or a new page:

  1. Fork the repository
  2. Edit or create a Markdown file in docs/en/
  3. Open a Pull Request

docs.title: Testing
docs.text: Download an ISO, install it on a real machine or VM, and report what you find. Issues can be reported on the forum or by opening a GitHub issue.

docs.title: Reviews
docs.text: A review on SourceForge helps other users discover the project and gives visibility to the community's work.

docs.title: Social media
docs.text: Share, comment, show your setup. Find us on Instagram, X and YouTube.

docs.title: Is CapivaraOS free?
docs.text: Yes, completely. It's an open source project — free to download, install and use.

docs.title: What's the difference between Marsh, Pup and Snout?
docs.text:
The difference is the desktop environment:

  • Marsh uses KDE Plasma — full-featured and highly customizable
  • Pup uses Xfce — lightweight, great on modest hardware
  • Snout uses GNOME — clean, no layout tweaks

The base system, the visual identity, the two exclusive applications (COS Dev Center and COS Config Center) and the development toolkit are the same across all three.

docs.title: Does CapivaraOS replace Fedora?
docs.text: Not exactly. CapivaraOS is built on top of Fedora — it inherits Fedora's package system, release cycle and hardware compatibility, but adds a visual identity of its own, two exclusive applications and a development environment ready at first boot.

docs.title: Can I install Fedora packages on CapivaraOS?
docs.text: Yes. Since the base is Fedora, all Fedora repositories and packages work normally. DNF and Flatpak are both available.

docs.title: Does CapivaraOS support Flatpak?
docs.text: Yes, Flatpak comes pre-configured. You can install apps from Flathub normally.

docs.title: How often are updates released?
docs.text: CapivaraOS follows Fedora's cycle. Security and package updates arrive continuously, through the software centre or dnf.

docs.title: Do I have to reinstall to get the next version?
docs.text:
No, from Series 2 on. The system moves between versions and generations in place, without reformatting, and takes a snapshot first so you can go back. See Keeping your system updated.

Series 1 is the exception: it does not have that path and needs a clean install — this is the last time.

docs.title: How do I know the ISO I downloaded is really yours?
docs.text: Every ISO ships with its SHA-256 and with a signature of that checksum, made with our key. The checksum proves the file arrived intact; the signature proves who published it. The steps are in Verify your download.

docs.title: Does local AI send my data anywhere?
docs.text: No. The models run on your machine, with no cloud and no account. The only thing that leaves your network is the initial model download. Details in COS Dev Center.

docs.title: Where do I report a problem?
docs.text: On the forum or by opening an issue on GitHub. See the Contribute page.

docs.title: Does CapivaraOS work in a virtual machine?
docs.text:
Yes, it works in VirtualBox, VMware and QEMU/KVM. For Marsh and Snout, we recommend enabling 3D acceleration.

In a virtual machine, local AI runs on the CPU — it works, but it is slow.

docs.title: Can I use CapivaraOS in dual boot?
docs.text: Yes. The Anaconda installer supports manual partitioning for dual boot with Windows or other Linux distributions.

docs.title: COS Config Center
docs.text:
COS Config Center handles, in a graphical interface, nine things that on Linux normally take the command line. It is exclusive to CapivaraOS and ships preinstalled on all three desktop editions.

To open it, look for COS Config Center in the application menu.

It asks for the administrator password only for settings that touch the system, and always warns first.

docs.title: Codecs and extra repositories
docs.text:
Enables the RPM Fusion repositories and Flathub, and installs the codecs Fedora cannot ship by default for patent reasons. This is what makes video and music "just play".

These are third-party repositories

RPM Fusion and Flathub are run by their own communities, not by CapivaraOS or Fedora. Some formats are covered by patents in certain countries — worth checking what applies where you live.

docs.title: Free disk space
docs.text:
Shows what can safely be removed, split into two lists: what lives in your user account (trash, thumbnails, unused Flatpak runtimes, container images) and what lives in the system and needs the password (already-installed packages, old logs, crash dumps).

Each item shows how much it takes before you decide. Nothing is removed unless you tick it.

docs.title: Disks at startup
docs.text: Mounts your extra disks and partitions automatically when the computer starts, without you editing /etc/fstab by hand.

docs.title: System log size
docs.text: Caps how much space system logs may use, so they do not grow forever and fill the disk.

docs.title: System check
docs.text:
A quick health check: disk space, running services, the video driver in use and errors since the machine booted.

At the end it builds a report to paste on the forum when you ask for help. The report does not include your name, the computer's name or network addresses.

docs.title: Brazilian keyboard
docs.text:
Choose between ABNT2, US International and US — and, on US International, enable typing ç with ' followed by c, the detail that most annoys anyone writing Portuguese on a US keyboard.

The same layout can be applied to the login screen as well.

docs.title: Language and formats
docs.text:
Separates two things that usually come glued together: the language of menus and applications, and the formats for date, number and currency. You can run the system in English while keeping Brazilian date and currency.

It applies system-wide, login screen included, and takes effect after you log out and back in.

docs.title: Firewall
docs.text:
Shows what is open to the network in plain words — "share folders on the network", "remote terminal access", "web server" — instead of port numbers.

There is also strict mode, which closes ports above 1024 and lets through only what you turned on.

docs.title: Remote access and network
docs.text:
Changes the computer name on the network, turns SSH remote access on or off, creates your SSH key and configures encrypted DNS.

Two caveats in this release

SSH password login stays enabled — we do not alter sshd_config. And encrypted DNS can break names that only exist on your local network; if something stops resolving after you enable it, switch back to "Automatic".

docs.title: About this release
docs.text:
COS Config Center ships with Series 2 as 0.11.x, a first public release with these nine modules. 1.0.0 will come after feedback from the people using it.

Not in this release: the NVIDIA driver (that is COS Dev Center's job), dual boot configuration and video acceleration.

System updates do not go through here either — those belong to the software centre or dnf. See Updating the system.

docs.title: COS Dev Center
docs.text:
COS Dev Center opens by itself at first boot and asks what you need. Instead of hunting for a tutorial to install local AI, Node.js or Docker, you pick from a list and it does the work — asking for the administrator password only when it genuinely has to.

It is exclusive to CapivaraOS and ships on all three desktop editions. To open it later, look for COS Dev Center in the application menu.

Install to disk before using it

Several items download multiple gigabytes. In a live session (running from the USB stick) space is limited and everything is lost at shutdown. Install the system first.

docs.title: Local AI
docs.text:
Installs the stack to run AI models on your own machine, with no cloud and no account:

  • Ollama — the engine that runs the models
  • Alpaca — a graphical interface to talk to them
  • Continue — the extension that brings AI into the editor

This downloads several gigabytes

On Fedora 45 the ollama package depends on ollama-rocm, the AMD GPU support. It gets installed even on machines with no AMD card, and it alone is a few gigabytes. This is not our choice: it is how the package is built in Fedora. Make room and give it a decent connection.

Without a dedicated GPU the models run on the CPU. That works, but it is slower — prefer smaller models.

docs.title: Language tracks
docs.text:
Installs languages in your user account, through mise, without touching the system:

Web/JavaScript (Node.js) · Python · Go · Rust · Java

Because nothing goes into the system, you can keep different versions per project and remove everything without a trace. Open a new terminal after installing, or your PATH is still the old one.

docs.title: Enable GPU (NVIDIA)
docs.text:
Installs the proprietary NVIDIA driver and CUDA from RPM Fusion, to accelerate local AI.

It is NVIDIA only. On AMD cards the acceleration already comes with local AI, through ROCm. With no dedicated GPU there is nothing to enable — AI runs on the CPU.

docs.title: Dev tools
docs.text:
You choose which ones to install:

  • VS Code — Microsoft's editor (system-wide, asks for the password)
  • Cline — an AI agent inside the editor
  • Open WebUI — a web chat interface for Ollama, in a podman container
  • Docker CE — containers (system-wide, asks for the password)

docs.title: GitHub CLI + pre-commit
docs.text: Sets up gh, for using GitHub from the terminal, and installs a pre-commit template with security checks that run before every commit: gitleaks (looks for leaking secrets), key detection and ShellCheck on scripts.

docs.title: How it behaves
docs.text:
One task at a time. While an installation runs, the others are blocked — this keeps two package transactions from fighting over the system.

The "Installed" section shows what you already installed through it, so you do not repeat yourself.

The password is asked only when needed. Language tracks and Open WebUI live in your user account and ask for nothing. VS Code, Docker and the NVIDIA driver touch the system and do ask.

docs.title: There is also COS Config Center
docs.text: The Dev Center takes care of the development environment. For system settings — codecs, keyboard, language, firewall, disks, network — the application is COS Config Center.

docs.title: Marsh
docs.text:
Desktop: KDE Plasma 6.8 · Base: Fedora 45 · Architecture: x86_64

Marsh is the flagship edition of CapivaraOS. KDE Plasma is one of the most customisable desktops on Linux, and Marsh arrives with it already arranged: global menu bar at the top, dock at the bottom, dark theme, and the project's visual identity from boot to desktop.

It is the most feature-rich of the three, and the one that asks the most of the machine.

docs.title: What ships with it
docs.text:
• KDE Plasma 6.8 on a Wayland session
  • Firefox as the default browser
  • LibreOffice, with Portuguese translation
  • VLC for video and audio
  • KeePassXC for passwords
  • Snapper, for Btrfs snapshots
  • COS Dev Center and COS Config Center, exclusive to CapivaraOS

docs.title: For developers
docs.text: COS Dev Center opens at first boot and sets up the workstation: local AI running on your own machine, per-user language tracks, dev tools and GitHub configured — no terminal.

docs.title: Visual identity
docs.text:
Theme, icons, Plymouth and GRUB coherent from boot to desktop, with a wallpaper collection of our own. On Marsh the wallpaper changes by itself with the time of day.

Switching between light and dark

Switch through Colors, in System Settings, not through the Global Theme — Breeze's stock Global Theme overrides our settings and undoes part of the identity.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: See Hardware requirements. Marsh is the heaviest of the three; on more modest machines, Pup delivers the same toolkit with a lighter desktop.

docs.title: Upgrading
docs.text: From Series 2 on, Marsh upgrades without reinstalling, from one version to the next and from one series to the following. See Updating the system.

docs.title: Pup
docs.text:
Desktop: Xfce 4.20 · Base: Fedora 45 · Architecture: x86_64

Pup is the light edition. Xfce uses little memory and runs well on older machines, but here it is not a cut-down version: Pup ships the same development toolkit as the other two editions.

It is the choice for modest hardware, and also for anyone who simply prefers a more direct desktop.

docs.title: What ships with it
docs.text:
• Xfce 4.20
  • Firefox as the default browser
  • LibreOffice, with Portuguese translation
  • VLC for video and audio
  • Snapper, for Btrfs snapshots
  • COS Dev Center and COS Config Center, exclusive to CapivaraOS

Pup is deliberately lean: heavy applications are left out by default and you install what you want.

docs.title: For developers
docs.text:
COS Dev Center opens at first boot with the same offering as the other editions — local AI, language tracks, dev tools and GitHub.

Local AI on a modest machine

Local AI downloads several gigabytes and, without a dedicated GPU, runs on the CPU. On an older computer that works, but it is slow: prefer smaller models, or skip this item.

docs.title: Visual identity
docs.text: The same identity as the other editions — Plymouth, GRUB, icons and theme — with a wallpaper collection of our own, including one exclusive to Pup.

docs.title: Upgrading
docs.text:
From Series 2 on, Pup upgrades without reinstalling. See Updating the system.

On Pup, upgrade from the terminal

dnfdragora, Xfce's default updater, does not list CapivaraOS updates on Fedora 45. This is not a problem with our repository — it is dnfdaemon failing the signature check. Until that is resolved, use sudo dnf upgrade in a terminal. Details in Updating the system.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: See Hardware requirements. Pup asks the least of the three editions.

docs.title: Snout
docs.text:
Desktop: GNOME 51 · Base: Fedora 45 · Architecture: x86_64

Snout is the clean edition. GNOME comes with no layout modifications — the experience is the one GNOME's developers designed — with the CapivaraOS identity applied on top: icons, theme, Plymouth and wallpapers.

It is the choice for people who like GNOME as it is.

docs.title: What ships with it
docs.text:

  • Firefox as the default browser
  • LibreOffice, with Portuguese translation
  • VLC and GIMP
  • Thunderbird for email
  • Snapper, for Btrfs snapshots
  • COS Dev Center and COS Config Center, exclusive to CapivaraOS

docs.title: Visual identity
docs.text: Curated extensions, an icon set of our own and an exclusive wallpaper collection — including one only Snout has. GNOME's layout is left untouched.

docs.title: Upgrading

docs.title: Herd by CapivaraOS
docs.text:
Herd is the server line of CapivaraOS: a headless Linux system (no graphical desktop), based on Fedora 44, meant to run on physical servers, virtual machines and the cloud — with a Brazilian identity, sane security by default, and Cockpit as the browser-based administration console.

Community Edition 1.0.1

This documentation covers Herd Community, the free and open-source edition. Architecture x86_64 (aarch64 support arrives in 1.1).

docs.title: The idea: herd = fleet
docs.text: In CapivaraOS, capybaras live in a herd — and that is how we think about servers: a fleet that works together. Herd delivers a predictable, hardened and easy-to-administer server base, whether it is a single node or many.

docs.title: What's in Herd Community
docs.text: Area What you get Base Fedora 44 (same generation as the Marsh/Pup/Snout 1.x desktops) Profile Headless server — no desktop, minimal surface Web console Cockpit at https://<ip>:9090 (services, network, storage, accounts, logs, terminal) Security SELinux enforcing, restrictive firewalld, hardened SSH, password policy, umask 027 Compliance herd-compliance-scan — built-in OpenSCAP report (SSG standard profile) Cloud cloud-init on the qcow2 image (key/network/user injection) Languages pt_BR and en_US; ABNT2 keyboard; America/Sao_Paulo timezone (adjustable)

docs.title: Two ways to install
docs.text:
• Installer ISO (bare-metal)

    To install on a physical server or VM from scratch, with the Anaconda text installer.

    Install via ISO

  • qcow2 image (cloud/VM)

    To spin up quickly on cloud or virtualization, with cloud-init handling the user, SSH key and network.

    Cloud/VM deployment

docs.text:
1. Requirements — what the server needs.
  2. Download and verify — get the image and check its integrity.
  3. Install via ISO or cloud/VM.
  4. Getting started — access, network, updates.
  5. Web console (Cockpit) — administer from the browser.

docs.title: Support and community
docs.text:
Questions, bugs and suggestions: see the Support page. Herd Community is community-maintained — your participation is welcome.

Content produced with AI assistance, under continuous review. Found an error? Open an issue.

docs.title: Administration
docs.text: Day-to-day tasks for a Herd server, from the terminal. Almost everything is also available in Cockpit, graphically.

docs.title: Updates
docs.text:
Herd uses dnf (Fedora base):

sudo dnf upgrade --refresh          # everything
sudo dnf upgrade --security         # security fixes only
sudo dnf check-update               # see what's new

Reboot after a kernel update: sudo systemctl reboot.

docs.title: Services (systemd)
docs.text:
systemctl status sshd               # a service's state
sudo systemctl restart sshd         # restart
sudo systemctl enable --now nginx   # enable at boot and start now
systemctl list-units --type=service --state=running

A service's logs: journalctl -u sshd.

docs.title: Logs (journal)
docs.text:
journalctl -b                       # current boot
journalctl -p err -b                # errors only
journalctl -u <service> -f          # follow in real time
journalctl --since "today"

docs.title: Storage
docs.text:
lsblk                               # disks and partitions
df -h                               # filesystem usage
sudo lvs; sudo vgs; sudo pvs        # LVM (the default install uses LVM)

To add/expand disks, LVM and mounts, the Storage module in Cockpit is the simplest path.

docs.title: Network
docs.text:
Managed by NetworkManager (nmcli) — see examples in Getting started › Network.

nmcli device status
nmcli connection show
ip a                                # current addresses

docs.title: Firewall (firewalld)
docs.text:
By default the public zone allows ssh, cockpit and dhcpv6-client.

sudo firewall-cmd --list-all                                   # zone state
sudo firewall-cmd --permanent --add-service=https              # allow a service
sudo firewall-cmd --permanent --add-port=8080/tcp             # allow a port
sudo firewall-cmd --reload                                     # apply

Allow a port only from an administration network (safer than opening to everyone):

sudo firewall-cmd --permanent --zone=internal --add-source=192.168.10.0/24
sudo firewall-cmd --permanent --zone=internal --add-service=cockpit
sudo firewall-cmd --reload

docs.title: SELinux
docs.text:
Ships in enforcing (recommended to keep):

getenforce
sudo ausearch -m avc -ts recent     # recent denials
sudo sealert -a /var/log/audit/audit.log   # analysis (if setroubleshoot installed)

Don't disable SELinux

If a service is blocked, prefer fixing the correct context/boolean rather than disabling SELinux. Disabling it removes an important containment layer.

docs.title: Web console (Cockpit)
docs.text: Herd ships with Cockpit, a browser-based administration panel. You can view system health, manage services, network, storage, accounts, read logs and even open a terminal — without installing anything extra.

docs.title: Access
docs.text:
Open in your browser:

https://<server-ip>:9090

Self-signed certificate

On first access the browser warns about the certificate (self-signed). That's expected on a freshly installed server — proceed. For production, you can install your own certificate in /etc/cockpit/ws-certs.d/.

The service is activated on demand (cockpit.socket): it only starts when someone accesses port 9090, which is already allowed in the firewall.

docs.title: Login
docs.text:
• Use a system user with its password (the same login as the console).
  • Root is blocked in Cockpit by default — use the administrator user (wheel group) you created.

Administrative access

After logging in, click "Turn on administrative access" (top corner) and enter the password again. This unlocks actions that require privilege (installing updates, managing services, storage, etc.).

docs.title: What you can do
docs.text: Module For what Overview Health (CPU, memory), system identity, time, hostname Logs Browse the journal (filter by priority, service, period) Storage Disks, partitions, LVM, filesystems, mounts Networking Interfaces, IP, firewall, bonds/bridges/VLANs Accounts Create/edit users, groups, SSH keys, password expiration Services Enable/stop/restart systemd units, view status Software updates Apply security and system updates Terminal The server shell right in the browser

docs.title: CapivaraOS identity
docs.text: Herd's Cockpit ships with the CapivaraOS branding (login screen and header) and without documentation links pointing to third parties — the docs link leads to this documentation.

docs.title: Security tip
docs.text:
Cockpit is a powerful administration door. On internet-facing servers, consider:

  • Accessing it over VPN or an SSH tunnel instead of exposing 9090 publicly: 
    ssh -L 9090:localhost:9090 user@<ip>
# then open https://localhost:9090 on your PC
  • Restricting the source in firewalld (allow 9090 only from the administration network).

See Security and compliance.

Image File When to use Installer ISO CapivaraOS-HERD-1.0.1-x86_64.installer.iso Install on a physical server or VM from scratch qcow2 disk CapivaraOS-HERD-1.0.1-x86_64.qcow2 Spin up quickly on cloud/virtualization with cloud-init

  • SourceForge: CapivaraOS-HERD/1.0.1 folder

docs.title: Verify integrity
docs.text:
Always check the SHA-256 of the downloaded file against the published value. Both image sums are in the SHA256SUMS file, in the same download folder:

395d06472e47b9b572769fe35f295806da01abb6536a89e5b5b82a0ec757776b  CapivaraOS-HERD-1.0.1-x86_64.qcow2
3a38b869c4f8b883e35de2fe2126d2f90b84b244f4c81481e67414e78a8d0d71  CapivaraOS-HERD-1.0.1-x86_64.installer.iso
Linux / macOSWindows (PowerShell) 
# download SHA256SUMS into the same folder, then run:
sha256sum -c SHA256SUMS
# it should answer "OK" for the file(s) you downloaded

Get-FileHash .\CapivaraOS-HERD-1.0.1-x86_64.installer.iso -Algorithm SHA256
# compare the output with the value above

If the checksum doesn't match

Do not use the image. A different hash means a corrupted download or a tampered file — download it again, preferably from the official source.

A checksum does not say who made the file

It proves the download arrived intact. To confirm the software is really ours, check the GPG signature — Verify the software is ours.

docs.title: Getting started
docs.text: After installing, these are the initial tweaks for a Herd server. Everything here can be done from the terminal (SSH/console) or from Cockpit.

docs.title: Access
docs.text:
• SSH (by key): ssh user@<ip> — remember SSH is key-only (see Install via ISO › Remote access).
  • Console: physical/IPMI, with the admin user or root.
  • Cockpit: https://<ip>:9090 (user + password).

docs.title: Elevate privileges (sudo)
docs.text:
The administrator user (wheel group) uses sudo:

sudo dnf upgrade --refresh

docs.title: Update the system
docs.text:
First things first — bring the system up to date:

sudo dnf upgrade --refresh
sudo systemctl reboot   # if a new kernel was installed

docs.title: Hostname
docs.text: sudo hostnamectl set-hostname herd-01.example.com

docs.title: Network
docs.text:
The network comes up via DHCP. For a static IP, use NetworkManager (nmcli):

# list connections and the interface
nmcli connection show
nmcli device status

# set a static IP (adjust connection name and values)
sudo nmcli connection modify "System eth0" \
  ipv4.method manual \
  ipv4.addresses 192.168.0.10/24 \
  ipv4.gateway 192.168.0.1 \
  ipv4.dns "1.1.1.1 8.8.8.8"

sudo nmcli connection up "System eth0"

Via Cockpit

You can do the same under Networking in Cockpit, with a graphical interface.

docs.title: Timezone and time
docs.text:
timedatectl                              # current state
sudo timedatectl set-timezone America/Sao_Paulo

Time synchronization (chronyd) is already active.

docs.title: Locale / language
docs.text:
The system ships pt_BR.UTF-8 and en_US.UTF-8. To change the default:

localectl                                # current state
sudo localectl set-locale LANG=en_US.UTF-8

docs.title: Users and SSH keys
docs.text:
Create another administrator:

sudo useradd -m -G wheel mary
sudo passwd mary
# add their public key:
sudo install -d -m 700 /home/mary/.ssh
echo "ssh-ed25519 AAAA... mary@pc" | sudo tee -a /home/mary/.ssh/authorized_keys
sudo chown -R mary:mary /home/mary/.ssh
sudo chmod 600 /home/mary/.ssh/authorized_keys

You can also manage accounts under Accounts in Cockpit.

docs.text:
firewalld only allows SSH and Cockpit by default. For a web service, for example:

sudo firewall-cmd --permanent --add-service=http --add-service=https
sudo firewall-cmd --reload
sudo firewall-cmd --list-all

docs.title: One-command hardening
docs.text:
Herd already ships hardened by default. When you need to go beyond the baseline — to meet a specific standard like CIS or PCI-DSS — herd-harden applies an entire compliance profile in one command.

It's the "apply" counterpart of herd-compliance-scan (which only reports): it uses the same Fedora SCAP Security Guide (SSG) content and applies remediation through Ansible.

By default it changes NOTHING

Without --apply, herd-harden runs a dry-run (Ansible check mode): it shows what would change without touching the system. It only applies for real with an explicit --apply. Always review the dry-run first.

docs.title: Available profiles
docs.text:
Profile Target Rules (approx.) Note standard Herd baseline (default) ~76 Already applied out of the box ospp Protection Profile for general-purpose OS (NIAP/Common Criteria) ~208 The "official" (non-draft) profile cis-l1 CIS Level 1 — Server ~324 SSG draft for Fedora cis-l2 CIS Level 2 — Server ~438 Draft; more aggressive pci PCI-DSS v3.2.1 ~121 Controls for cardholder environments

You can also pass the full technical profile id (xccdf_org.ssgproject.content_profile_*). List them all with herd-harden --list.

What to expect from each standard — no false promises

  • STIG: there is no DISA STIG profile for Fedora (the SSG only ships it for RHEL). If your requirement is DoD-adjacent, ospp is the closest baseline.
  • CIS: the CIS profiles for Fedora are community-maintained drafts in the SSG (CIS does not publish an official Fedora benchmark). Useful and solid, but treat them as what they are.
  • PCI-DSS: the embedded profile is v3.2.1.
  • Herd delivers the controls and the evidence — it makes the system compliance-ready. Compliance itself is process, legal and organization; no OS declares itself "certified" on your behalf.

ospp and cis change the crypto — watch out for ed25519 keys

The ospp and cis profiles enable the FIPS crypto-policy, which rejects ed25519 SSH keys (and ciphers outside the FIPS set). On a server reached over SSH, make sure you have an RSA or ECDSA key before applying and test a fresh login right after --apply, without closing your current session — herd-harden itself warns about this at the end. Details on the Security and compliance page.

docs.title: 1. See what would change (dry-run)
docs.text:
sudo herd-harden cis-l1

This generates the profile's remediation playbook and runs Ansible in check mode (--check --diff): you see every proposed change, nothing is applied.

docs.title: 2. Apply
docs.text:
sudo herd-harden cis-l1 --apply

Changes are applied to this server. Output also goes to a log:

/var/log/herd-harden-<date>.log

docs.title: 3. Verify the result
docs.text:
Measure before/after with the scanner, on the same profile:

sudo herd-compliance-scan cis-l1

docs.title: Other commands
docs.text:
herd-harden --list      # list the datastream profiles
herd-harden --help      # short help

Start with the lightest

A good progression is standard → ospp → cis-l1 → pci (or cis-l2, the most restrictive). Apply one at a time, always reviewing the dry-run and testing your services afterward — higher profiles harden the surface quite a lot.

docs.title: Cautions
docs.text:
• Run the dry-run first. High profiles may restrict something your application depends on. Review the --diff before --apply.
  • Test after applying. Confirm SSH, your services, and Cockpit.
  • herd-harden requires ansible-core (already on Herd). The playbook is generated from the vendored datastream — it works offline.
  • Specific settings you don't want a profile to overwrite should go in your own drop-ins (see Adjust).

docs.title: Third-party credits and licenses
docs.text:
Like herd-compliance-scan, herd-harden uses Fedora's SCAP Security Guide (ssg-fedora-ds.xml, BSD-3-Clause, © 2012-2017 Red Hat, Inc.). License details on the Security and compliance page. Profile names come from the SSG itself; "CIS" refers to the Center for Internet Security benchmarks — Herd only runs the corresponding profiles, without reproducing the benchmark text.

docs.title: Cloud / VM deployment (qcow2)
docs.text:
The qcow2 image already ships cloud-init and qemu-guest-agent, which makes it ideal for spinning up quickly on cloud, KVM/libvirt, Proxmox and the like. cloud-init handles the user, SSH key, hostname and network on first boot.

Image = template

The qcow2 is a template. Each VM created from it is personalized by cloud-init on first boot (from the datasource).

docs.title: Option A — KVM/libvirt with a NoCloud seed
docs.text: Without a cloud provider, the simplest way to feed cloud-init is a NoCloud datasource: a small ISO with two files, meta-data and user-data.

docs.title: 1. Create the seed files
docs.text:
meta-data:

instance-id: herd-01
local-hostname: herd-01

user-data (note the #cloud-config on the first line):

#cloud-config
users:
  - name: admin
    groups: [wheel]
    sudo: "ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD:ALL"
    shell: /bin/bash
    ssh_authorized_keys:
      - ssh-ed25519 AAAA... you@machine
# optional password — used for CONSOLE and Cockpit (SSH is key-only)
chpasswd:
  expire: false
  users:
    - name: admin
      password: "change-this-password"
      type: text

SSH is key-only

Herd ships with PasswordAuthentication no. Include your public key in ssh_authorized_keys, otherwise you won't get in over SSH. The password (if set) is for the console and for Cockpit.

Passwordless sudo

The example uses NOPASSWD:ALL (sudo without a password prompt) — handy in cloud with key-only login. For tighter control, switch to ALL=(ALL) ALL and set a user password; then sudo will require it.

docs.title: 2. Build the seed ISO
docs.text:
genisoimage -output seed.iso -volid cidata -joliet -rock user-data meta-data
# (or: cloud-localds seed.iso user-data meta-data)

docs.title: 3. Launch the VM
docs.text:
cp CapivaraOS-HERD-1.0.1-x86_64.qcow2 herd-01.qcow2

virt-install --name herd-01 --memory 2048 --vcpus 2 \
  --disk path=herd-01.qcow2,format=qcow2,bus=virtio \
  --disk path=seed.iso,device=cdrom \
  --os-variant fedora-unknown --import \
  --network network=default,model=virtio --graphics none

Find the IP (virsh domifaddr herd-01) and connect: ssh admin@<ip>.

docs.title: Option B — Cloud provider
docs.text:
1. Upload the qcow2 as an image/template in your provider (OpenStack Glance, etc.) — or import it as a disk (Proxmox: qm importdisk).
  2. Create the instance from the image.
  3. Provide the user-data (same #cloud-config as above) through the provider's mechanism (metadata service / ConfigDrive). cloud-init applies it on first boot.

qemu-guest-agent

Already installed and enabled — the virtualization host can query the IP, quiesce snapshots and shut down gracefully.

docs.title: Install via ISO (bare-metal)
docs.text:
This guide covers installing Herd Community on a physical server or a VM using the installer ISO. The installer is Anaconda in text mode — ideal for headless servers, with no dependency on a graphical interface.

Offline installation

The ISO is self-contained: packages are embedded, so the installation does not need internet access.

docs.title: 1. Prepare the boot media
docs.text:
Write the ISO to a USB drive (≥ 2 GB) or mount it as virtual media (iDRAC/iLO/IPMI, or the VM's "CD/DVD").

Linux/macOS (dd)WindowsVM 
lsblk   # find the USB device (e.g. /dev/sdX)
sudo dd if=CapivaraOS-HERD-1.0.1-x86_64.installer.iso of=/dev/sdX bs=4M status=progress oflag=sync

Confirm the device

dd on the wrong disk erases data irreversibly. Check with lsblk first.

Use Balena Etcher or Rufus (DD/image mode).

Point the VM's CD/DVD drive to the .iso file. No need to burn a USB drive.

docs.title: 2. Boot from the ISO
docs.text:
Enter the server's boot menu (usually F11/F12/Del/Esc) and select the media. The CapivaraOS GRUB menu appears — choose Install Herd by CapivaraOS.

Anaconda starts in text mode and shows a numbered menu. Items marked [x] are already configured; those marked [ ] need your attention.

docs.title: 3. Configure the required items
docs.text: The profile comes ready (pt_BR + en_US locale, ABNT2 keyboard, America/Sao_Paulo timezone, DHCP network, offline installation source). You need to set:

docs.title: Disk (installation destination)
docs.text:
Choose the number for "Installation Destination", select the disk and confirm automatic partitioning (or define your own).

Partitioning

Automatic uses LVM and works for most cases. For specific layouts (e.g. separate /var, quota sizes), configure manually.

docs.title: Root password
docs.text: Set it under "Root password". Direct root login over SSH is disabled by default (see Security); the root password is for the console (physical/IPMI) and recovery.

docs.title: Create an administrator user
docs.text:
This step matters — it is the account you'll use day to day and in Cockpit (Cockpit blocks root login).

  1. Choose the number for "User creation".
  2. Type 1 to create the user — the form expands.
  3. Fill in the user name and password.
  4. Mark Administrator ([x]) — this puts the account in the wheel group (allows sudo and enabling administrative access in Cockpit).
  5. Type c to continue.

docs.title: 4. Begin the installation
docs.text: Back on the main menu, with all items [x], type b (begin) to install. When it finishes, remove the media and reboot.

docs.title: 5. First boot
docs.text:
In the GRUB menu you'll see the Herd entry. The system boots to text mode and prints, on the console, the Cockpit address:

Herd by CapivaraOS 1.0.1  ·  headless server (Fedora 44)
Web console: https://<ip>:9090/

docs.title: 6. Remote access — read this
docs.text:
By default SSH accepts keys only (PasswordAuthentication no). That means right after installing you cannot log in over SSH with a password. Options:

  • Console first (recommended): log in at the physical/IPMI console with the admin user and add your public key: 
    install -d -m 700 ~/.ssh
echo "ssh-ed25519 AAAA... you@machine" >> ~/.ssh/authorized_keys
chmod 600 ~/.ssh/authorized_keys
    Then: ssh user@<ip>.
  • Cockpit: the web console at https://<ip>:9090 accepts user + password (it is not SSH) — you can administer without a key. See Web console.
  • Really need SSH by password? You can relax the policy, with security caveats — see Security › Adjusting SSH.

docs.text: Herd Community 1.0.1 ships for x86_64 (64-bit). aarch64 (ARM) support arrives in version 1.1.

Component Minimum Recommended Architecture x86_64 (64-bit) x86_64 CPU 1 core 2+ cores RAM 1 GB 2 GB or more Disk 10 GB 20 GB or more Network 1 Ethernet interface — Firmware Legacy BIOS or UEFI UEFI

Real server vs. testing

docs.title: Security and compliance
docs.text: Herd is hardened by default — a freshly installed server comes with a sensible security profile, with no configuration needed from you. This page explains what's enabled, how to audit, and how to adjust.

docs.title: What's hardened
docs.text: Area Herd default SELinux enforcing Firewall firewalld allowing only SSH and Cockpit (plus dhcpv6-client); mdns off SSH key-only; no root; login attempt limits (see below) Passwords quality minimum (pwquality) and password aging umask 027 on login sessions (new files aren't world-readable) Packages gpgcheck=1 (signature verification in dnf)

docs.title: SSH — default policy
docs.text:
File: /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/50-capivaraos-herd.conf

PermitRootLogin no
PasswordAuthentication no
PermitEmptyPasswords no
KbdInteractiveAuthentication no
X11Forwarding no
MaxAuthTries 3
LoginGraceTime 30
AllowAgentForwarding no

docs.title: Password policy
docs.text:
• Quality — /etc/security/pwquality.conf.d/50-capivaraos-herd.conf: minimum length 12, at least 3 character classes, no long repeats/sequences.
  • Aging — /etc/login.defs: maximum 90 days, minimum 7 days.

Ciphers (crypto policy)

SSH and TLS ciphers/MACs/KEX follow the system crypto-policy (already strong by default on Fedora), rather than values hardcoded in Herd.

docs.title: Audit: herd-compliance-scan
docs.text:
Herd embeds an OpenSCAP scanner with Fedora's SCAP Security Guide content. Run:

sudo herd-compliance-scan

This evaluates the system against the standard profile and generates:

/root/herd-compliance-<date>.html      # readable report (open in a browser)
/root/herd-compliance-<date>.xml       # XCCDF results (machine)
/root/herd-compliance-<date>.arf.xml   # ARF: re-renderable evidence / auditing

To list available profiles or run another one (it accepts the same aliases as herd-harden — standard, ospp, cis-l1, cis-l2, pci — or the full id):

herd-compliance-scan --list
sudo herd-compliance-scan ospp

ARF is the evidence

The .arf.xml is the machine-readable format that bundles datastream + results together: you can regenerate the report later without re-scanning, and it's what auditing/aggregation tools consume.

Copy the report to your PC

scp user@<ip>:/root/herd-compliance-*.html .
(or open the file via Cockpit's Terminal/Files.)

Why standard is the default

The standard profile is a balanced baseline: it closes what matters (SSH, firewall, SELinux, password, umask) without breaking ordinary services. That is why it runs by default.

The stricter profiles — cis-l1, cis-l2, ospp and pci — ship with the system and run with one command, no licence and nothing to install:

sudo herd-harden cis-l2        # dry-run by default
sudo herd-harden cis-l2 --apply

They change a great deal more (CIS Level 2 evaluates 438 rules against 76 in standard) and can break services you rely on. Run the dry-run first, read what would change, and decide — it is your call, not an edition limit.

docs.title: Verify the software is ours
docs.text:
The image checksum proves the file arrived intact — see Download and verification. It does not prove who produced it: anyone who replaced the image would publish the new checksum alongside it. The GPG signature is what answers that question.

None of this asks you to trust us. These are four checks you run yourself.

docs.title: 1. Is the key installed?
docs.text:
The public key ships inside the system and is imported by the repositories RPM:

rpm -q gpg-pubkey --qf '%{SUMMARY}\n' | grep -i capivaraos

docs.title: 2. Does the fingerprint match?
docs.text:
This is the step that matters. Compare what is on your machine against the value published here:

gpg --show-keys --with-fingerprint /etc/pki/rpm-gpg/RPM-GPG-KEY-capivaraos-herd

The fingerprint must be exactly:

C852 6722 0A81 18C9 864F  0648 BE5B 82AD C8A2 85C0

If it does not match

Stop. A different key means the system trusts someone who is not us. Do not apply updates, and report it through the private security channel.

The Herd key is separate from the one used by the desktop editions (75FA 3340 40FD 0150 4AAD 9337 E07F 78EA 4070 11BD). Compromising one does not compromise the other.

docs.title: 3. Are the installed packages signed?
docs.text:
# signature of a downloaded RPM, before installing
rpm -K ./some-package.rpm
# expected: ...: digests signatures OK

# who signed an already installed package
rpm -qi capivaraos-herd-hardening | grep -i signature

An unsigned package, or one signed by another key, shows up as NOT OK, MISSING KEYS or (none).

docs.title: 4. Does the repository require signatures?
docs.text:
grep -E 'gpgcheck|repo_gpgcheck' /etc/yum.repos.d/capivaraos-herd.repo

Both must be 1. gpgcheck validates each package; repo_gpgcheck also validates the repository metadata — without it, someone controlling the server could advertise a different package list, even without being able to sign the packages themselves.

makecache is not the test

On dnf5, dnf makecache only warns when metadata is badly signed, and still exits 0. The transaction is what refuses it. To test for real, try an actual operation (dnf check-update or dnf update) — that is where a tampered repository is rejected.

docs.title: Why this holds even if the server falls
docs.text: The private key has never been on the repository server. It is generated in an offline ceremony and kept in a vault; it enters a machine only at the moment of signing a release, and is removed afterwards. So a compromised server can at most serve files your system will refuse, because there is no way to sign them. That is why the trust sits in the key, not in whoever hosts it.

docs.title: Adjust
docs.text: All configuration comes from the capivaraos-herd-hardening package. You can override it to match your policy.

docs.title: SSH — enable password (with a caveat)
docs.text:
Think twice

SSH password authentication increases the attack surface (brute force). Prefer keys. Only enable password auth if you really need it, and combine it with fail2ban/firewall source limits.

Create a drop-in that comes after ours (alphabetical order):

sudo tee /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/60-local.conf >/dev/null <<'EOF'
PasswordAuthentication yes
EOF
sudo systemctl restart sshd

docs.title: Adjust password rules
docs.text:
sudo tee /etc/security/pwquality.conf.d/60-local.conf >/dev/null <<'EOF'
minlen = 14
EOF
# aging: edit /etc/login.defs (PASS_MAX_DAYS / PASS_MIN_DAYS)

docs.title: Add your SSH key
docs.text:
install -d -m 700 ~/.ssh
echo "ssh-ed25519 AAAA... you@machine" >> ~/.ssh/authorized_keys
chmod 600 ~/.ssh/authorized_keys

Planning to apply ospp/cis or FIPS mode? Don't rely on ed25519

These profiles switch the system crypto-policy to FIPS, which does not accept ed25519 keys (nor ciphers outside the FIPS set). Generate an RSA (ssh-keygen -t rsa -b 3072) or ECDSA (ssh-keygen -t ecdsa -b 384) key before hardening and confirm a fresh login. For the default baseline, ed25519 is still great. See One-command hardening.

docs.title: Production best practices
docs.text:
• Expose the minimum: only the necessary ports in firewalld.
  • Access Cockpit over VPN/tunnel, not open to the internet.
  • Keep the system updated (dnf upgrade) — Fedora security updates.
  • Run herd-compliance-scan periodically and address what makes sense for your environment.

docs.title: Encryption at rest and FIPS (optional)
docs.text: Two reinforcements that are off by default (so they don't get in the way of headless servers and cloud), which you enable when your policy calls for them.

docs.title: Disk encryption (LUKS)
docs.text:
Protects data at rest (a stolen/discarded disk leaks nothing). It's an install-time decision. Since the Herd installer is text-mode (no "Encrypt my data" checkbox from the graphical version), encryption is set via the kickstart — since 1.0.1 the cryptsetup package ships in the ISO payload, so an encrypted install works offline. Use the Herd kickstart template:

clearpart --all --initlabel
autopart --type=lvm --encrypted --passphrase=YOUR-PASSPHRASE

Point the installer at that kickstart either by building your own ISO (KS=my.ks ./build-iso.sh, see the repository) or by passing inst.ks=<url> at boot.

Verify afterward:

lsblk                       # the device should show up as "crypt"
sudo cryptsetup status luks-<uuid>

Headless server: the passphrase is asked at boot

A LUKS volume prompts for the passphrase on every boot. Without a console (physical/IPMI/serial), the machine won't come up on its own after a reboot. For server auto-unlock, use NBDE — clevis with TPM2 (local seal) or Tang (key over the network). Do not use LUKS on the cloud image (qcow2).

docs.title: FIPS mode
docs.text:
FIPS 140 forces the use of validated cryptographic modules only and restricts the allowed algorithms. Useful for government/sector requirements.

Fedora 44 no longer ships fips-mode-setup

Fedora removed fips-mode-setup. FIPS is now turned on with fips=1 on the kernel command line — preferably at install time (enabling it afterward "has subtle bugs and is no longer recommended", per Fedora). The initramfs already ships the fips module and the crypto-policy switches to FIPS on its own when the kernel is in FIPS mode.

Recommended — at install: on the ISO boot menu, edit the entry (e/Tab) and append fips=1 to the kernel line. The installed system boots in FIPS.

Post-install (with the caveat above): on Herd /boot is a separate partition, so fips=1 must be paired with boot=UUID=<uuid of /boot>. This block detects the UUID for you:

if findmnt /boot >/dev/null 2>&1; then
  UUID=$(sudo blkid -s UUID -o value "$(findmnt -no SOURCE /boot)")
  ARGS="fips=1 boot=UUID=$UUID"
else
  ARGS="fips=1"
fi
sudo grubby --update-kernel=ALL --args="$ARGS"
sudo reboot

Verify:

cat /proc/sys/crypto/fips_enabled     # 1 = active
update-crypto-policies --show          # FIPS

To disable: remove fips=1 (sudo grubby --update-kernel=ALL --remove-args="fips=1") and reboot.

Test access before relying on it

FIPS mode restricts algorithms: in particular, ed25519 SSH keys stop being accepted (use RSA or ECDSA), along with ciphers and certificates outside the approved set. Confirm SSH login on a second session right after rebooting, before closing the access you have.

docs.title: FAQ
docs.text:
Can I log in over SSH with a password right after installing?

No — SSH is key-only (PasswordAuthentication no). Add your key via the console/Cockpit, or (with caveats) enable password auth per Security › SSH.

Does Cockpit accept root login?

No. Use the administrator user (wheel group) and click Turn on administrative access.

Is there an ARM (aarch64) version?

Not yet in 1.0.1 — aarch64 support arrives in 1.1.

Can I use it in commercial production?

Yes. The software is free (GPLv3) and can be used for any purpose, including commercial. Only the trademark (name/logo) is protected — see the repository's TRADEMARK.md.

How do I set up a web server/database/container?

Herd is a lean server base. Install what you need with dnf (nginx, podman, postgresql-server, etc.) and open the ports in the firewall.

docs.title: 1. Download the ISO
docs.text: Go to the download page and choose your distro: Marsh, Pup or Snout.

docs.title: 2. Check what you downloaded
docs.text:
Before writing it, check the ISO's SHA-256. It is quick, and it rules out the most common reason for a USB stick that will not boot: a corrupted download.

If you want to be sure not only that the file arrived intact but that it is ours, check the signature too. The steps are in Verify your download.

docs.title: 3. Flash to a USB drive
docs.text:
You'll need a USB drive with at least 4 GB. We recommend Fedora Media Writer or balenaEtcher — they write the image straight to the drive and just work:

  • Fedora Media Writer (Windows, macOS, Linux) — Fedora's official tool, the best choice
  • balenaEtcher (Windows, macOS, Linux) — simple, three clicks
  • dd (Linux/macOS, via terminal):
sudo dd if=capivaraos-marsh-2.0.0.iso of=/dev/sdX bs=4M status=progress

Be careful with dd

Check the correct device with lsblk before running the command. Overwriting the wrong device is irreversible.

If Ventoy hangs at startup

Ventoy keeps several ISOs on one stick and works in most cases, but on some computers the live session never comes up: the boot stays stuck at "Starting CapivaraOS…", sometimes with a message like Can't create /lib/dracut/hooks/.../99-ventoy-….sh. Ventoy loads the ISO over loopback and injects that script into the boot — the error is Ventoy's, not the image's. When that happens, write the ISO straight to the stick with Fedora Media Writer, balenaEtcher or dd, and boot again.

docs.title: 4. Boot from USB
docs.text:
Restart your computer and enter the boot menu (usually F12, F2 or Del during startup). Select the USB drive.

In the menu you will see CapivaraOS \<edition> 2 45 — the 2 is the CapivaraOS version and the 45 is the Fedora release it is built on.

docs.title: 5. Try or install
docs.text:
When it boots, you'll see the option to enter live mode (try without installing) or start the installation directly.

Try it first, if you can

Live mode runs from memory and does not touch your disk. It is how you confirm that wireless, sound and video work on your machine before installing anything.

docs.title: 6. Follow the installer
docs.text:
CapivaraOS uses the Anaconda installer, the same one used by Fedora. It will guide you through:

  1. Language — the system ships ready in Brazilian Portuguese and English; you pick during installation and can change it later in COS Config Center
  2. Disk partitioning — the default is Btrfs, which is what makes the snapshots before each upgrade possible
  3. User account creation
  4. Installation

Encrypting the disk

If you choose encryption (LUKS), the computer will ask for the disk password at every boot, on a screen with the capybara. Keep that password: without it there is no way to open the disk.

docs.title: 7. First boot
docs.text:
Remove the USB drive and reboot. At first login COS Dev Center opens by itself and asks what you want to install — local AI, languages, dev tools. None of it is mandatory: you can close it and open it later from the menu.

From then on the system stays up to date without reinstalling. See Keeping your system updated.

Hit a problem? Post on the forum or open an issue on GitHub.

CapivaraOS is based on Fedora and inherits its hardware compatibility. Intel and AMD processors are supported, with experimental ARM support.

Live mode

docs.title: Verify your download
docs.text:
Before you write the USB stick, it's worth checking the file you downloaded. There are two different questions, each with its own answer:

  • Did the file arrive intact? → the SHA-256 checksum.
  • Is the file really ours? → the GPG signature.

The first catches a corrupted or half-finished download (the most common reason an ISO won't boot). The second proves the image was published by CapivaraOS and not swapped by someone else. The second step is optional, but it's quick and recommended.

docs.title: What to download
docs.text:
In each edition's folder (capivaraos.org/en/download.html or SourceForge), next to the ISO you'll find:

File What it's for CapivaraOS-<Edition>-2.0.0-x86_64.iso the image ...iso.sha256 the published checksum ...iso.sha256.asc the GPG signature of the checksum ...iso.torrent BitTorrent download (verifies itself as it goes)

The torrent already verifies for you

If you download via the .torrent, your BitTorrent client checks every piece against its hash while downloading — a torrent download that finishes is already intact. The GPG signature (below) is still worth doing.

docs.title: 1. Did the file arrive intact? (checksum)
docs.text:
Download the .sha256 into the same folder as the ISO and run:

Linux / macOSWindows (PowerShell) 
sha256sum -c CapivaraOS-Snout-2.0.0-x86_64.iso.sha256
# should answer: CapivaraOS-Snout-2.0.0-x86_64.iso: OK

(on macOS use shasum -a 256 -c if you don't have sha256sum.)

Get-FileHash .\CapivaraOS-Snout-2.0.0-x86_64.iso -Algorithm SHA256
# compare the output with your edition's value in the table below

The published 2.0.0 values are:

Marsh   79666af3bee34b6ad9477c3e4f49aee5e0d621931b80163bb88e30dc2b03dd22
Pup     13acef6ce12cb0120f5cdb8890ef2d3a5f7607e324516611afe4cfb4a481209f
Snout   8e25df502c4a22b6ac898fde9347aa03c47a28220a2bcdd83dc1981e5e212bd1

If the checksum doesn't match

Don't use the image and don't write the stick — a different hash means a corrupted or tampered file. Download it again, preferably via the torrent, which verifies itself.

docs.title: 2. Is the file really ours? (GPG signature)
docs.text:
The checksum proves the file arrived intact, but not who published it: anyone who swapped the image would publish a matching checksum too. The signature answers that. The .sha256.asc is the GPG signature of the checksum file, made with our key. Its private half was generated in an offline ceremony and is kept in a vault: it enters a machine only at the moment of signing a release, and is removed afterwards.

a) Download and import our public key:

curl -O https://repo.capivaraos.org/RPM-GPG-KEY-capivaraos
gpg --import RPM-GPG-KEY-capivaraos

b) Check the fingerprint. This is the step that matters — it must be exactly:

75FA 3340 40FD 0150 4AAD  9337 E07F 78EA 4070 11BD

gpg --show-keys --with-fingerprint RPM-GPG-KEY-capivaraos
# uid: CapivaraOS (repo signing key) ... <capivaraos-bot@users.noreply.github.com>

If the fingerprint doesn't match

Stop. A different key means the file is signed by someone who isn't us. Don't write the image and report it through the security channel.

c) Verify the signature on the checksum (both files in the same folder):

gpg --verify CapivaraOS-Snout-2.0.0-x86_64.iso.sha256.asc \
             CapivaraOS-Snout-2.0.0-x86_64.iso.sha256
# expected: Good signature from "CapivaraOS (repo signing key) ..."

The WARNING: This key is not certified with a trusted signature message is normal: it only means you haven't signed our key in your own web of trust. What matters is the Good signature and the fingerprint you checked in step (b).

The same key signs your updates

It's the same key that signs the installed system's update repository. Check the fingerprint once and you recognize both the ISO and the updates.

docs.title: Next step
docs.text: File intact and signature verified? Head to the Installation guide to write the stick and install.

docs.title: Keeping your system updated
docs.text:
An installed CapivaraOS stays up to date without reformatting and without waiting for a new ISO. There are two kinds of update, with different tools:

Kind What changes Tool Day-to-day updates fixes and new program versions, within the same generation the app store or dnf upgrade Generation upgrade jump to the next generation of the system (new Fedora base) capivaraos-upgrade

In both, besides Fedora's packages you receive our packages (branding, COS Dev Center, themes, fixes) from a signed repository. Trust doesn't depend on trusting the server: every package and the metadata are verified against our GPG key (gpgcheck + repo_gpgcheck). The private half of that key is kept in a vault and only enters a machine at the moment of signing a release. It's the same key from verifying your download.

docs.title: Day-to-day updates
docs.text:
These arrive on their own through each edition's app store — just apply them when they show up:

Edition Where Marsh (KDE) Discover Snout (GNOME) GNOME Software Pup (Xfce) from the terminal — see the warning below

From the terminal, on any edition, this always works:

sudo dnf upgrade --refresh

Pup: update from the terminal

On the Fedora 45 base, Xfce's graphical updater may not list our updates (a limitation of that component, not of our repository). On Pup, prefer sudo dnf upgrade --refresh — it's the reliable path until the graphical updater is fixed upstream.

docs.title: Generation upgrade (in-place)
docs.text:
When a new generation of CapivaraOS is published, you jump to it without reinstalling, using capivaraos-upgrade. It uses dnf5's offline transaction (system-upgrade): it downloads everything while the system is running and applies it on the next boot, in an isolated environment.

It's built not to surprise you: by default it only checks, and downloading and rebooting are separate, explicit steps.

# 1. Pre-flight: shows what would happen. Downloads and reboots nothing.
capivaraos-upgrade

# 2. Download the transaction (system stays up; no reboot):
sudo capivaraos-upgrade download

# 3. Apply: reboots and performs the upgrade in the offline environment.
sudo capivaraos-upgrade reboot

Fails closed: it won't leave you half-upgraded

The upgrade only proceeds if our signed repository already exists for the target generation. If it doesn't yet, it refuses — otherwise the machine would move to the new Fedora base and leave the CapivaraOS packages (branding, COS Dev, themes) behind. So running capivaraos-upgrade today will usually answer that no target is published yet: that's the correct behavior, not an error.

docs.title: Before the upgrade: a snapshot
docs.text:
When the disk supports it, the tool takes a snapshot first, so you can roll back:

  • btrfs + snapper: automatic snapshot. This is the installer's default arrangement on all three editions.
  • LVM: not automatic — the tool prints the manual command (lvcreate -s …) in the pre-flight.
  • No compatible storage: nothing is snapshotted — back up first.

The pre-flight tells you what will happen on your machine

No need to guess which case you are in: run capivaraos-upgrade with no arguments. It reports whether a snapshot will be taken, and under what conditions, before anything is downloaded.

docs.title: If you need to go back
docs.text:
The snapshot the tool creates shows up in the list described as "pré capivaraos-upgrade" — that is your return point:

sudo snapper list

To undo the file changes from that point to now:

sudo snapper undochange <snapshot#>..0

The 0 means "the current state". To revert the whole system after a generation upgrade, the path is to boot the snapshot and promote it — undochange reverts file changes, it does not swap the system over.

On LVM, the rollback is sudo lvconvert --merge <snapshot> followed by a reboot.

docs.title: Why Series 1 doesn't upgrade to Series 2
docs.text: Series 1 has reached end of life and has neither the signed repository nor the in-place upgrade engine (both were born in Series 2). There is therefore no in-place jump from Series 1 to Series 2: if you're on Series 1, do a clean install of Series 2 — see verifying your download and the installation guide. Back up your data first. The Series 1 documentation is still available in the Archive.
